facts.note: §6.2 (outturn) page 6; §10.3-10.4 (mid-year) page 13. Note the paper's §10.3 states investments at 31.3.25 as '£288m' — this contradicts the §6.2 table (£188m) and appears to be a drafting slip that mixes the internal borrowing figure into the investments narrative. Do NOT raise externally. Mid-year total corroborated by counterparty list totalling £264.6m at 4.58%. Includes a £15m loan to Hillingdon Council for 277 days at 5.20%.

facts.value: £89.3m at 31.3.2025, down from £119.7m at 31.3.2024. A further £20m repaid since 1 April 2025 — implied ~£69.3m today.

source.title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2025/26 — Council, 28 January 2026

facts.note: §13.7-13.8, page 18. Paper describes 'correspondence with a few banks that provide its LOBO loans to see if there were any opportunities to reschedule the debt'. §13.8 states 'in the last two years the Council has reduced its LOBO loans from £119.7m to £89.3m as at 31 March 2025' — cross-referring to §6.1's Other Market Loans line (£119.7m at 31.3.24, £89.8m at 31.3.25) the £30.4m reduction sits almost entirely in 2024/25. Plus £20m since 1 April 2025 = £50.4m total run-off, all inside the 28 months from 31.3.24 to today. The 'Other Market Loans' line at §6.1 (£89.8m at 31.3.25) sits £0.5m above the £89.3m LOBO figure, so essentially the whole market-loan line is LOBO. This is the most active LOBO run-off in the councils we have read; the pattern elsewhere is lenders exercising options and being refused (Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York, Harrow, Wolverhampton, Staffordshire, Newport, Bridgend).

summary.text:
Lewisham's 28 January 2026 report combines the 2024/25 outturn with a 2025/26 mid-year review, in a single Council paper (no appendix carrying the numbers separately). All the substantive tables sit in the covering document. The paper is unusually stale for a Council item — mid-year figures are at 30 June 2025 and the MUFG interest-rate forecast is dated 11 August 2025, so members are voting on data five to seven months old.

Two things stand out. First, §13.7-13.8 discloses an active LOBO run-off: £119.7m at 31 March 2024, £89.3m at 31 March 2025, and a further £20m repaid since 1 April 2025 — an implied ~£69.3m today, and £50.4m of LOBO principal off the book since March 2024. Of the councils we have read, every other LOBO story is a lender exercising an option and being refused (Kent, Tameside, York, Newcastle, Harrow, Wolverhampton, Staffordshire, Newport, Bridgend, Bath and North East Somerset). Lewisham is the only one negotiating repayment directly. Second, internal borrowing grew £115m in the year (£173.3m to £288.3m) while cash investments fell £128m (£316m to £188m) — the balance sheet identity ties to the pound, and §13.1 states the under-borrowed position is deliberate. Financing costs to net revenue jump from 16.0% to 18.2% in 2025/26 before easing.

The PWLB loan-book reconciliation FAILED. Paper (§6.1, 31.3.2025) prints Public Works Loan £90.5m at 4.3%. Our file holds 29 loans totalling £138.6m at 4.38%. Rates roughly agree but the £48m gap in principal is too large to attribute purely to Start-date artefacts and likely reflects post-year-end drawdowns not captured against the outturn. Per pipeline rules, no loan-book claim is quoted in the email; the LOBO story and the internal-borrowing / cash-draw story carry the draft.

officer.subject: £50m of LOBOs off your book — nobody else in the library is negotiating repayment
officer.body:
Hi Katharine,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your January outturn and mid-year report, offered ahead of the next treasury item. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The LOBO paragraph in particular is one of the more informative we've read.

The part I'd start with is §13.8. Your LOBOs went from £119.7m at 31 March 2024 to £89.3m at 31 March 2025, and you disclose a further £20m repaid since 1 April 2025 — implying roughly £69m today, about £50m off the book since March 2024. Of the councils we've read, every other LOBO story is a lender exercising an option and the council refusing to pay the new rate — Dexia at Kent and Tameside in the same window, KBC at Bath and North East Somerset going floating with six-monthly resets, and refused calls at Harrow, Wolverhampton, Staffordshire, Newport, York and Bridgend. Lewisham is the only one we've read that is negotiating repayment directly with the LOBO banks. The run-off you describe is the most active in the library.

The other thing that jumps out is the balance sheet at §6.4. Internal borrowing rose from £173.3m to £288.3m across the year — a £115m increase — and cash investments fell £128m over the same period (£316m to £188m at §6.2). §13.1 says the under-borrowed position is deliberate while investment returns sit below borrowing cost, which is coherent on today's curve. The headline financing-cost ratio at §13.19 steps from 16.0% in 2024/25 to 18.2% in 2025/26 before easing to 15.7%; the ex-PFI series climbs steadily from 4.9% to 6.9%.

The MUFG forecast at §8.1 is dated 11 August 2025 and had the 25-year PWLB certainty rate at 5.50% for Q3 2026, with the 50-year at 5.30%. Today's 25-year certainty is 6.46% and the 50-year 6.27% (PWLB notice 314/26, PM fixing on 14 August) — the long end is running about a point above where the paper's forecast had it. Not a criticism of the forecast; a mark of where the burden of the £72.8m of 2025/26 prudential borrowing (§12.3) falls if the curve stays where it is.

For where to look, pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows the whole sector's monthly PWLB draws with rate and maturity — worth a look before committing to a tranche in a thin week. And pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices any council's PWLB book against the DMO's repayment curve daily. Indicative only, only the DMO can quote, and we don't model MRP or accounting treatment.

On training, three look relevant. LOBO loans, given how live the topic is in your book. Cost of carry and internal borrowing, given the size of the £288m position and the strategy at §13.1. And the liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes, and §13.21-13.25 sits at the middle of that conversation. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
